title: Why Great Teams Question Themselves
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership post argues that overconfidence and busyness keep many teams from examining their own assumptions, and that the research on team reflexivity shows this is costly. Team reflexivity is the habit of stepping back to ask how the team is working together, what is not working and whether to change approach, and teams that do it routinely outperform those that presume they are on track. The authors note that momentum hides problems and that reflection pays off most when it is least convenient, for example when a team is struggling and tempted to just work harder. They recommend building reflection into the rhythm of work through project-phase debriefs, a standing weekly question and milestone reviews. Candor depends on the leader going first by admitting mistakes, asking what they are missing and thanking people who deliver uncomfortable news.
points: Teams that periodically reflect on their coordination and impact outperform those that assume everything is on track.
Busy teams build momentum, and momentum hides problems because people stop questioning the plan and mistake activity for progress.
Reflection delivers the biggest gains when teams are struggling, which is exactly when they are most tempted to skip it.
Build reflection into routine through end-of-phase debriefs, a standing weekly question and short reviews after milestones.
Leaders enable candor by going first: acknowledging mistakes, asking what they are missing and thanking those who say uncomfortable things.
quotes: The research is clear. Teams that periodically reflect on their own coordination and impact outperform those that presume everything is on track.
This practice is called team reflexivity, and it refers to the habit of stepping back and asking, “How are we working together?” “What isn’t working?” “Should we change our approach?
Unfortunately, momentum hides problems. In teams that are heads down, people stop questioning the plan and mistake activity for progress.
Perhaps surprisingly, reflection pays off most when it feels least convenient. Reflexivity delivers its biggest gains when teams are struggling or underperforming.
Teams take their cue from their leader, and nothing signals that honest reflection is welcome faster than a leader who goes first.
Without that example, it is too easy for reflection to become a politeness ritual where everyone agrees things are mostly fine.
Momentum will carry a team a long way, but only reflection tells it whether it’s going the right way.
